newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dollar skips to near 5-year high on yen in Tokyo.
newsitem.headline: Dollar skips to near 5-year high on yen in Tokyo.

text.p: News of surprisingly strong growth in the U.S. economy helped send the dollar skipping to a nearly five-year high against the yen in Tokyo on Thursday morning.
It also helped stocks amass hefty gains as investors snapped up blue-chip shares on the Tokyo bourse.

Both markets were buoyed by Wednesday's release of data showing the U.S. economy grew by an annual rate of 5.6 percent during the first three months of this year, its fastest pace in more than nine years.

This set off a wave of buying in the U.S. stock market overnight, with the Dow Jones Industrial index rising above the 7,000 level for the first time since March 13 to unofficially close at 7,009. U.S. Treasury bonds also traded higher.

Heartened by these gains, the dollar crept higher from the start of Tokyo morning trade. It briefly touched a high of 127.18 yen in mid-morning, its highest level since August 1992, but then dropped back slightly in relatively quiet trade.

Currency dealers said many in the market were keen to sell dollars in order to avoid hitting "knock-out" options points near 127.30 yen, and that this, despite talk of a huge amount of stop-loss buying orders near 127.20 yen, was likely to keep the dollar from advancing strongly during Asian trading time.

These options would give holders the right to buy dollars at 123 or 124 yen, well below current levels, unless the dollar touches the knock-out price of 127.30 yen before the expiry date, traders said. Holders of the options are rumoured to be selling the dollar when it nears 127 yen, in order to prevent their option positions from being knocked out, and this is helping to limit the dollar's rise.
The options positions will expire in New York later on Thursday, but dealers are divided on whether this leaves the dollar free to rise unrestrained.

Additional downward pressure was expected from sales interest by major exporters near 127.50 yen, along with concern about the chance of the Bank of Japan intervening in the market to sell dollars if the greenback starts rising aggressively.
But slides are unlikely, with institutional investors eager to buy dollars on any dips. The greenback was stalled at 127.11/13 yen by midday.
The yen's weakness helped stocks power ahead, with the Nikkei average of 225 leading shares up 310.63 points or 1.62 percent at 19,461.75 by the lunch break.
"Investors bought shares backed by firm earnings, lifting the index past its closing high for the calendar year," said Hisao Suzuki, Yamaichi Securities deputy general manager.

Brokers said the yen's fall was a plus for shares of electronic and high-tech firms, which are exporters. Blue-chip favourite Sony Corp hit a new high for the calendar year of 9,300 yen, or about $73, but slipped back to 9,240 yen at midday.

The benchmark Nikkei rose past the January 6 closing high of 19,446.00 to 19,558.36 in the two-hour morning session. It was the highest intra-day rise since December 24, when the index ascended to 19,699.74.

Brokers said short-covering of cash stocks also helped boost the Nikkei. "U.S. hedge funds actively bought Nikkei futures on Wednesday, so there was a need to cover cash shorts this morning," a broker at Okasan Securities.
Foreign investors showed strong interest in buying dollars, and brokers said pension funds were poised to buy on dips, giving the market additional psychological support.
